posts.author: mrpaslow
posts.content_md:
Hi all,

I've been lurking for a few months off and on, and I'm glad to see that holography is still alive. I was doing a good bit of holography back in the late 80's and early-to-mid 90's, but haven't had lab-space since then. The highlight of that time was attending the 1991 symposium in Lake Forest 

Now I might have lab-space soon and I want to get back into things.

I'm really intrigued by the idea of making my own silver halide plates, and I've been reading with interest Jeff Blythe's diffusion method. Seems rather straight-forward, if I can find a place to purchase the requisite chemicals. On the other hand, I found this paper: [http://www.iop.org/EJ/article/0950-7671 ... i9p333.pdf](http://www.iop.org/EJ/article/0950-7671/31/9/307/siv31i9p333.pdf)

and I'm wondering if any of you will comment, and if it might be possible to use Jeff's method with the chemical set mentioned in the paper, or some combination thereof. 5000 lines/mm would work fine for me, I guess.

Also Jeff mentions using certain polymers for his diffusion process. What polymers? Are there any details about that available? 

Thanks,

Dan

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md: In my opinion, the Crawford paper and subsequent booklet are the best places to start (in English) if you want to make a holographic emulsion by using the double-jet method. Of course, it's more involved than the diffusion method described by Blyth. However, preparing a finished silver halide emulsion prior to coating (double-jet) would, I think, give the final coated emulsion superior uniformity.

posts.author: jean
posts.content_md:
I've tried the double-jet method and frankly, imho, the diffusion method is as far as I know, better (at least for hobbyiests). With the doubje-jet method, you must deal with grain grown problem, you need a grain grown restrainer but quality and source of the gelatin play a role too. You need a solution of low concentration gelatin (1 or 2%) to get suffisantly small grains but coating is less easy (of course, you can add gelatin after rippening to raise concentration and then use curtain veil or meyer bar coating but this operation can produce grain growing. And last but not least, hardening of gelatin can be a challenge.

As you can guess, I didn't enjoy results of my several tests of double-jet method. Maybe someone else should have better results than I, I hope.

But for me, it's definitively the diffusion method who get my preference.

Maybe a day... 

...I'll be back !!!

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
The diffusion method has always been of interest to me, but I decided to pursue the double-jet method because the diffusion method involves three applications of liquid material, and three drying cycles for the emulsion:

1. Coat with gelatin, dry

2. Apply nitrate, dry

3. Apply bromide/dye and sensitizer, dry

Hopefully others who have tried the diffusion method can clarify this (I haven't tried it yet) but it seems to me (and for my purposes) that there are too many opportunities for irregularities in the emulsion to develop. I think Dr. Blyth once stated that his process was designed for people who wanted to do it for the fun of making their own silver-halide holographic emulsion. I don't think it was ever claimed that it could routinely produce flawless emulsion layers, which is essentially what we would expect with a commercial emulsion.

I would hazard a guess that all commercial holographic emulsions are produced (and have been produced) by the double-jet method.

Jeff Blyth put up some cash to finance free distribution of the pinacyanol chloride, I tossed in the requirement that you had to be willing to post (preferably here) about your experiences with the process. I'm still wondering if a "kit" of sorts would be worth the trouble to set up for sale.

 -Gary

posts.author: jean
posts.content_md:
> **Joe:** I would hazard a guess that all commercial holographic emulsions are produced (and have been produced) by the double-jet method.

I know that Slavich uses the technique of double-jet and the freeze/thawn method to increase concentration of gelatin (and restrain grain growning)

Source : "Silver Halide emulsions for Lippmann photography and holography" - Hans I. Bjelkhagen - Proc. SPIE Vol. 1600, pp 44-59 (1991)

In this paper, article point out the technique used by H. Thiry to make holographic emulsion with grain size of about 20 nm. with the double-jet technique but seems that one of important point is the advance of silver nitrate over the potassium bromide (can result in finer grains).

If your goal is produce commercial emulsion, I wish you success.

I don't think it was ever claimed that it could routinely produce flawless emulsion layers, which is essentially what we would expect with a commercial emulsion.I would hazard a guess that all commercial holographic emulsions are produced (and have been produced) by the double-jet method.

Recently Scientists from Univ. of Applied Sciences from Berlin have optimized a 'Diffusion' + Double-Jet holographic emulsion "DESA" (Practical holography XIX SPIE) that is claimed far superior than Agfa or even BB plates, with a special coating method by "Thiry" and the Blyth diffusion method.

I think seriously that this method could be at least as perfect as the common available emulsions, with the advantage of a small or medium laboratory could self made it(!).

Hi Sergio.

I just went to SPIE and got both of the DESA papers, from Practical Holography XVIII and XIX. While the papers lack specific details, i.e. a "recipe", I think if used in conjunction with the Blythe and Crawford papers, a dedicated holographic hobbyist could probably make 10000lp/mm silver halide plates. If it was me, I might have some success by my third batch...maybe 

It's also interesting that they use (what I'm assuming is) a different dye for red-sensitization: 3-Carboxymethyl-3’, 9-diethyl-5,5’-dimethyl

thiacarbocyanine betaine. Sorry, I don't know the common name for this, I just took it out of the paper.

Well, I'm kinda psyched about all this. DESA are claiming they frequently get 80-100% diffraction efficiency. Man, the future's looking bright!

(I don't think we have to worry about an ultra-high-res end-user holo-printer any time soon)![:wink:](https://holographyforum.org//cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/twitter/twemoji@latest/assets/svg/1f609.svg) 

Dan
